newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan trade surplus set to take another dive.
newsitem.headline: Japan trade surplus set to take another dive.

text.p: Japan's politically sensitive merchandise trade surplus is likely to continue its slide in August as growth in imports is seen far exceeding that of exports, reflecting a structural shift in the economy.

Any likely drop in Japan's vast surplus, often the source of bitter rows with the United States, would be good news for Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, who is to meet U.S. President Bill Clinton on September 24 in New York.
The August trade data is to be released on September 18.
"Imports are expected to stay buoyant, although the tempo of their growth may be slowing," said Shuji Shirota, an economist at Yamaichi Research Institute of Securities and Economics.

A Reuters poll of analysts showed that the nation's customs-cleared surplus is projected to be between 160 billion yen ($1.45 billion) and 314 billion yen ($2.85 billion) in August after a surplus of 535.14 billion yen ($4.86 billion) a year earlier. The trade data is given only in yen terms.
Analysts expect the surplus to show a healthy year-on-year drop in August after a 37.7 percent plunge in July to 504.03 billion yen ($4.58 billion).
In the first 20 days of August the surplus nose-dived 81.1 percent from a year ago to 69.09 billion yen ($628 million).
"The interim numbers failed give any impression that exports are bound to recover remarkably in August," said Yoshito Sakakibara, an economist at Salomon Brothers Asia Ltd.

"I don't think exports will stay stagnant for a very long period of time, because there are signs that exports may be starting to gain some momentum. But you may not be able to see any clear recovery yet in August," Sakakibara said.
Japanese manufacturers are still carrying out structural changes after shifting their production bases abroad, and this would in turn put a damper on export growth, analysts said.
Price-sensitive consumers, meanwhile, tended to favour cheaper imported goods, especially from Asia, while companies were becoming more dependent on overseas suppliers.
Imports may have slowed in August, as there were fewer business days during the month than in August last year, but it could still post growth of 15.8 percent, said Shirota.
Exports, meanwhile, may show only single-digit growth, because a temporary boost in car exports to the United States, seen in July, is likely to have petered out in August, he said.
Analysts say the shrinkage will become less dramatic in the coming months.

"The tempo of year-on-year shrinkage in the surplus could slow to around 20 percent by the year's end. The rate could even slow to single-digit growth next fiscal year, but I don't think the surplus will start growing again during the year (ending March 1998)," he said.

Analysts said the pace of shrinkage in the surplus was slowed by the yen's sharp decline to 110 yen to the dollar from its record high of 79.75 yen marked in April 1995, which was helping manufacturers regain some competitiveness abroad.
A weak yen makes Japanese manufacturers more competitive as it makes their products cheaper in terms of foreign currency.

A weaker yen may take the steam out of imports by making them more costly in Japan, but analysts cast doubt on whether the currency factor alone could reverse the trend of a shrinking surplus, which has lasted for the past 20 months.
